semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ}: When the interrogative enters upon a negation it affirms it, so the meaning becomes: "We have indeed expanded"; that is why a past verb is conjoined to it. Similar to it is {أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيداً وَلَبِثْتَ} [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 18]. The majority read the ḥāʾ with the jussive (jazm) by «لم», and Abū Jaʿfar read it with fatḥa. Al-Zamakhsharī said: «They said: perhaps he articulated the ḥāʾ distinctly and gave it its full value at its point of articulation, so the listener thought he gave it fatḥa.» Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: «The original is "ألم نَشْرَحَنْ" with the light nūn [of emphasis]; then he replaced it with an alif, then omitted it for lightness», as Abū Zayd quoted:
4597 - مِنْ أيِّ يَوْمَيَّ من الموتِ أفِرّْ ... أيومَ لم يُقْدَرَ أم يومَ قُدِرْ
(From which of my two days shall I flee death: the day it is not decreed, or the day it is decreed?)
with fatḥa on the rāʾ of «لم يُقْدَرَ»; and like his saying:
4598 - اضْرِبَ عنكَ الهمومَ طارِقَها ... ضَرْبَكَ بالسيفِ قَوْنَسَ الفَرَسِ
(Strike away from you the cares that come by night, as you strike with the sword the crest of the horse.)
with fatḥa on the bāʾ of «اضربَ». End of quotation. This is built on the permissibility of emphasising [with the nūn] a verb made jussive by «لم», which is very rare, as in his saying:
4599 - يَحْسَبُه الجاهلُ ما لم يَعْلما ... شيخاً على كُرْسِيِّه مُعَمَّما
(The ignorant one, as long as he does not know, takes him for a turbaned elder on his chair.)
So this reading is composed of three bases, all of them weak: because emphasising a verb made jussive by «لم» is weak; replacing it [the nūn] with an alif belongs only to the pause, and treating continuous speech like the pause is contrary to the basic rule; and omitting the alif is weak, because it is contrary to the basic rule. The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] explained it according to a dialect that al-Liḥyānī related in his «Nawādir» from some Arabs, namely the jussive by «لن» and the subjunctive by «لم», the reverse of what is known among people, and he considered this better than the preceding. He quoted the saying of ʿĀʾisha bint al-Aʿjam praising al-Mukhtār, who rose to seek vengeance for al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both:
4600 - قد كادَ سَمْكُ الهدى يُنْهَدُّ قائمُهُ ... حتى أتيحَ له المختارُ فانْعَمدا
في كلِّ ما هَمَّ أمضى رأيَه قُدُماً ... ولم يُشاوِرَ في إقدامِه أحدا
(The roof of guidance had nearly had its pillar collapse, until al-Mukhtār was granted to it and it was propped up. In everything he resolved upon he carried out his judgement boldly, and consulted no one in his advance.)
with fatḥa on the rāʾ of «يُشاور», and he considered it open to both explanations.

semin-durr:3-3.t:
His saying: {أَنقَضَ ظَهْرَكَ}, i.e. it made it produce النقيض, which is the sound of cracking and coming apart because of its heaviness — a parable for what used to weigh upon him ﷺ. The lexicographers said: أَنْقَضَ الحِمْلُ ظَهْرَ الناقةِ (the load made the she-camel's back creak) when you hear a creaking from it because of the severity of the load; and سمِعْتُ نقيضَ الرَّحْلِ, i.e. its creaking. Al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās said:
4601 - وأَنْقَضَ ظهري ما تَطَوَّيْتَ منهمُ ... وكنتُ عليهم مُشْفِقاً مُتَحَنِّناً
(What you concealed against them made my back creak, while I was compassionate and tender toward them.)
And Jamīl said:
4602 - وحتى تداعَتْ بالنَّقيضِ حِبالُه ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(…until its ropes called out to one another with creaking…)

semin-durr:5-5.t:
His saying: {فَإِنَّ مَعَ العسر يُسْراً}: The majority read with sukūn on the sīn in the four words, and Ibn Waththāb, Abū Jaʿfar and ʿĪsā with ḍamma on it. There is disagreement about it: is it [the ḍamma form] original, or made heavy from the quiescent form? The alif and lām in the first «العُسر» are for the definiteness of the genus, and in the second for prior reference (ʿahd); that is why it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās: «One hardship will never overcome two eases»; and it is also related as a saying of the Prophet (marfūʿ) that he, peace be upon him, came out laughing, saying: «One hardship will never overcome two eases.» The reason for it is that when the Arabs bring a noun and then repeat it with the alif and lām, it is the same as the first, e.g. «جاء رجلٌ فأكرمْتُ الرجلَ» (a man came and I honoured the man), and as in His saying, the Exalted: {كَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَآ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ رَسُولاً فعصى فِرْعَوْنُ الرسول} [al-Muzzammil: 15–16]; and if they repeat it without alif and lām, it is other than the first. So in His saying: {إِنَّ مَعَ العسر يُسْراً}, when He repeated the second hardship He repeated it with «أل», and since the second ease is other than the first, He did not repeat it with «أل».
Al-Zamakhsharī said: «If you say: what is the meaning of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās? — and he mentioned what has preceded — I say: this is acting on the apparent sense and building on the strength of hope, and [on the principle] that Allah's promise is to be taken only in the fullest and most far-reaching sense the wording admits. What is to be said about it is that it is possible that the second clause is a repetition of the first, just as He repeated His saying: {وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلْمُكَذِّبِينَ} [al-Mursalāt: 15] to establish its meaning in the souls and fix it in the hearts, and just as the single word is repeated in your saying: "جاء زيدٌ زيدٌ" (Zayd came, Zayd); and it is possible that the first is a promise that hardship is inevitably followed by ease, and the second a new promise that hardship is followed by ease, so they are two eases on the supposition of a new statement. The hardship is one only because it must be either that its definiteness is for prior reference, namely the hardship they were in, so it is the same; because its rule is the rule of "زيد" in your saying: "إنَّ مع زيد مالاً، إنَّ مع زيد مالاً" (Zayd has wealth, Zayd has wealth); or that it is for the genus that everyone knows, so it is also the same. As for ease, it is indefinite, covering part of the genus; and if the second statement is a new one, not a repetition, it covers a part other than the first part, without any difficulty.»
Abū al-Baqāʾ said: «The hardship in the two places is one, because the alif and the lām require the repetition of the first. As for "يُسْراً" in the two places, they are two, because when an indefinite noun is meant to be repeated, its pronoun or the alif and lām is brought; and from here it was said: "One hardship will never overcome two eases".» Al-Zamakhsharī also said: «If you say: "مع" is for accompaniment, so what is the meaning of the accompaniment of ease and hardship? I say: He meant that Allah the Exalted would bring them ease after the hardship they were in, within a short time; so He brought the awaited ease near, until He made it as though it were joined to the hardship, as an increase in consolation and a strengthening of hearts.» He also said: «If you say: what is the meaning of this indefiniteness? I say: magnification, as though it were said: with hardship is a mighty ease, and what an ease! In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd it is [written] only once. If you say: if it is established in his reading unrepeated, why did he [the Prophet] say: "By Him in Whose hand is my soul, if hardship were in a hole, ease would seek it until it entered upon it; one hardship will never overcome two eases"? I say: it is as though by the two eases he intended the sense of magnification in His saying "يُسْراً", so he interpreted it as "the ease of the two abodes", and that is in reality two eases.»

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ}: The majority read «فَرَغْتَ» with fatḥa on the rāʾ, and it is the well-known [form]; Abū al-Sammāl read it with kasra, and it is a minor dialectal form; al-Zamakhsharī said: «It is not the eloquent one.» Al-Zamakhsharī [also] said: «If you say: how is His saying "فإذا فَرَغْتَ فانصَبْ" connected with what precedes it? I say: when He enumerated His past favours and His forthcoming promise, He urged him to gratitude and to striving in worship. From Ibn ʿAbbās: when you have finished your prayer, then exert yourself in supplication.»
The majority read with fatḥa on the ṣād and sukūn on the bāʾ, as an imperative from النَّصَب (toil). It was also read with doubling of the bāʾ, with fatḥa, as an imperative from الانْصباب (pouring forth). [Translator's note: the source has «متفوحة», evidently for «مفتوحة» (with fatḥa).] Likewise it was read with kasra on the ṣād and sukūn on the bāʾ, as an imperative from النَّصْب (setting up) with sukūn on the ṣād. I do not consider the first anything but a misreading of the dots (taṣḥīf), nor the second anything but a distortion (taḥrīf), for it is related from the Imāmiyya, and their interpretation of it is: when you have finished with prophethood, then appoint the caliph. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: «It is a weak, irregular (shādhdh) reading not established from any scholar.» Al-Zamakhsharī said: «Among the innovations is what is related from some of the Rāfiḍa, that he read "فانصِبْ", i.e. appoint ʿAlī to the imamate; and if this were valid for the Rāfiḍī, it would be valid for the Nāṣibī to read it thus and make it a command to النَّصْب, which is hatred of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, and enmity toward him.»

semin-durr:8-8.t: His saying: {فارغب}: from الرَّغْبة (desire). Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read «فَرَغِّب» with doubling of the middle radical, as an imperative from رَغَّبَه with doubling, i.e. make people desire to seek what is with Him. [Translator's note: the source writes the reading as «فَرَغَّب», but its own gloss «فَرَغِّب» shows the imperative form.]
